title: Some people think rejecting God’s Word protects them from it.
paragraphs: Some people think rejecting God’s Word protects them from it.
King Jehoiakim believed that.
And his story in Jeremiah 36 is one of the most chilling scenes in the Bible.
Because this king did something few people in Scripture ever dared to do.
He burned the Word of God.
But what happened next reveals a lesson every generation needs to hear.
The prophet Jeremiah had been warning Judah for years.
God told him to write down every prophecy He had spoken—every warning about the coming judgment of Babylon if the nation refused to repent.

Jeremiah dictated the message to his scribe, Baruch.
The scroll was read publicly in the temple.
The message spread quickly through Jerusalem.
Officials were shaken.
So they brought the scroll to the king.
This moment could have changed everything.

The nation was already on the edge of disaster.
If the king humbled himself, repentance could have spread through the land.
But Jehoiakim’s reaction revealed the true condition of his heart.
It was winter.
The king sat in his palace with a fire burning in a brazier beside him.
As the scroll was read aloud, something shocking happened.
After only a few columns were read…
Jehoiakim cut the scroll with a knife.
Then he threw the piece into the fire.
More of the scroll was read.
Again he cut it.
Again he burned it.
Piece by piece.
Line by line.
God’s message was thrown into the flames.
The Bible records something terrifying about this moment:

“Yet they were not afraid, nor rent their garments.”
— Jeremiah 36:24
In the ancient world, tearing your garments was a sign of repentance and fear before God.
But the king and his servants sat there calmly while God’s Word burned.
No trembling.
No humility.
No repentance.
Just defiance.
But here is the truth Jehoiakim did not understand.
Burning the scroll did not erase the message.
God spoke again.
Jeremiah was instructed to write another scroll.
And the Bible says something remarkable:

“And there were added besides unto them many like words.”
— Jeremiah 36:32
In other words…
The message didn’t disappear.
It became even stronger.
The king tried to silence God’s Word.
But heaven simply wrote it again.
This story is not just about an ancient king.
It is about the human heart.
Because many people today do something very similar.
They do not literally burn Scripture.
But they remove the parts they don’t want to hear.
They ignore the warnings.
They avoid conviction.
They reshape God’s message until it feels comfortable.
But truth does not change because we dislike it.
God’s Word is not fragile.
It does not depend on human approval.
Kings may reject it.
Cultures may mock it.
Generations may ignore it.
But what God speaks remains true.
Jehoiakim thought destroying the scroll gave him control.
But history shows the opposite.
Judah fell.
Babylon came.
Jerusalem was devastated.
And the king who burned God’s warning could not escape the consequences of ignoring it.
The fire in the brazier did not stop the fire of judgment.
There is a powerful lesson here.
Sometimes the most dangerous moment in a person’s life is when they hear God’s Word clearly—and still refuse to respond.
Not ignorance.
Not confusion.
But conscious rejection.
Jehoiakim heard the message.
He understood the warning.
And he chose contempt.
Yet even in this story, we see something incredible about God.
God did not owe Judah another warning.
But He sent one.
The scroll was written again.
The message returned.
That reveals something about the heart of God.
He continues to speak—even after people resist Him.
Warnings are not cruelty.
They are mercy.
Conviction is not condemnation.
It is an invitation to turn before it is too late.
So the question this story leaves us with is simple but serious.
What do we do when God’s Word confronts us?
Do we humble ourselves?
Or do we quietly cut away the parts we do not want to obey?
Because rejecting truth does not remove accountability.
Ignoring God does not silence Him.
And burning the scroll does not stop the message.
Three lines from this story should stay with us:

You can burn the scroll.
But you cannot burn the truth.

You can silence the messenger.
But you cannot silence God.

You can reject the warning.
But you cannot escape the consequences.
Jehoiakim tried to destroy the message.
But thousands of years later…
We are still reading it.
The scroll survived.
The Word remained.
And the lesson still speaks.

📖 Jeremiah 36:23–24
"And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire… yet they were not afraid."

Reflection Question:
If God confronted your life with a truth today, would you receive it… or would you try to burn the scroll?
